newsitem.title: USA: Chrysler, UAW talk all night, a sign strike may end.
newsitem.headline: Chrysler, UAW talk all night, a sign strike may end.

text.p: Chrysler Corp. and union negotiators continued talking Wednesday morning after an all-night bargaining session, officials from both sides said, a sign a nearly monthlong strike may soon be over.
"They're still at the table, and that's a good sign," said Chrysler spokesman Tony Cervone.

The talks were the most significant development in the dispute since nearly 1,900 members of the United Auto Workers union struck a big Chrysler engine plant here just before midnight on April 9. Talks resumed late Tuesday afternoon.
The strike has forced the nation's third-largest automaker to halt production of some of its most profitable models, including Dodge Ram pickup trucks and Jeep Grand Cherokee sport utility vehicles.
Industry analysts have said the strike has cost Chrysler $300 million in lost profits, an amount that grows $15 million to $20 million a day as the walkout drags on.
Union officials confirmed published reports that a broad understanding on a key issue in the strike, farming out work to outside sources, had been reached by senior negotiators.
But officials on both sides said numerous issues and details remained to be worked out.
"If there was a real hard and fast agreement, you would have seen it settled," one person familiar with the talks said.

UAW members have insisted Chrysler drop plans to shift production of drive shafts at the big Mound Road plant to an outside supplier, a practice known as outsourcing, that they say would result in the loss of about 300 jobs.
The Detroit Free Press and Detroit News reported Wednesday that company and union officials reached a broad agreement on the outsourcing issue.
The plant supplies most of the engines and rear-wheel drive components for Chrysler pickup trucks, Jeep Cherokees and Grand Cherokees, the Viper sports car, and other models.

Meanwhile, talks aimed at resolving two strikes against General Motors Corp. continued Wednesday. Those strikes have forced GM to halt production of its Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass cars in Oklahoma City and some pickup trucks at a plant in Pontiac, Mich.
